subtype: Approach: freezing because the plan was never practised [Pitfall]
passage: The smoke alarm shrieked at 2 a.m. Pradeep sat up. He knew there was a plan; Amma had read it out once in the living room, but he had never walked it. Now he stood frozen in his doorway with tears running down his face. The words swirled: stairs, low, door... which first? "Pradeep!" His mother Preeti rushed in, took his hand and said, "Low. Follow me." They went down the stairs together and out to the gate, where neighbours were already gathering. Pradeep shivered and sobbed. Afterwards he asked whether they could really walk the way out, tomorrow, all of it.

qa.q: What time did the smoke alarm go off?
qa.a: The smoke alarm shrieked at 2 a.m.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he stood in the doorway?
qa.a: Terrified and confused, so frozen that he cried, because the plan words swirled in his head.

qa.q: What could the family do now, and why?
qa.a: They could walk the escape route together, by day and once in the dark, so the steps become movements and not only words.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt when she found Pradeep standing there?
qa.a: Preeti was probably alarmed and protective, since she rushed in and took his hand straight away.

grounding: A child who only heard about an escape plan freezes at a real smoke alarm and needs a parent to lead him out.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: thinking of how the owner must feel [Thinking]
passage: On the school bus after the field trip, Kishore's foot bumped something under the seat: a brown wallet, thick with notes. His heart jumped. Enough for the new football boots! Then he pictured Papa patting an empty pocket at the vegetable market, the worry crossing his face. "Whoever lost this is patting their pocket right now," Kishore thought. "The boots matter less than that face." He carried the wallet to Elizabeth Ma'am at the front. "I found it under my seat." She thanked him and said the office would call the owner from the cards inside.

qa.q: Where did Kishore find the wallet?
qa.a: He found it under his seat on the school bus.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he pictured the owner patting an empty pocket?
qa.a: Sympathy and worry for the owner, which outweighed his wish for the boots.

qa.q: What else could Kishore do to help the owner find the wallet, and why?
qa.a: He could ask Elizabeth Ma'am how the school will let people know, so the owner can claim it.

qa.q: How might the person who lost the wallet feel when it is returned?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since that person had been worried about the missing money.

grounding: A boy finds a wallet on the bus, imagines the owner's worry, and decides returning it matters more than the money.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: handing it to a responsible adult [Action]
passage: When I was eleven, I, Lakshmi, found a wallet on the bus to school. Nobody was near. I could have put it in my bag and no one would ever know. Instead I walked to the conductor and handed it over. "There are cards inside," I told him. "They will show the owner's name." Then at school I went to Binita Miss and told her what I had done. Why both? I thought, if two grown-ups know, nobody can ever say Lakshmi took a single rupee. Binita Miss wrote it in the school diary and smiled. Two days later the owner came to thank the conductor, and I was proud in a quiet way.

qa.q: Who did Lakshmi give the wallet to on the bus?
qa.a: Lakshmi gave it to the conductor.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi worried about when she thought of telling two grown-ups?
qa.a: She wanted to be sure nobody could say she took anything, so she felt careful and wanted to be clear.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the plan work?
qa.a: She handed the wallet to the conductor and also told her teacher, so the cards could trace the owner and she was covered.

qa.q: How did Binita Miss see what Lakshmi had done?
qa.a: Binita Miss took it as a responsible act, writing it in the school diary and smiling.

grounding: A girl gives a found wallet to the conductor and tells her teacher, so the cards can lead to the owner.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
passage: In the corridor after school I saw Yash pick up a folded wad of notes. He sat on the steps, took out his rough notebook, and I peeked. Two columns. Under KEEP: cricket bat. Under GIVE BACK: what if they are counting on it for the doctor, or the flat's rent? And below that, in small letters: I will remember it every time I swing. He chewed his pencil for a long time. I can't tell whether he was more tempted or more scared. Then he stood up, walked to the office, and Hansa Ma'am, the clerk, took the notes and wrote his name in the register. - Mahima

qa.q: What did Yash write under KEEP?
qa.a: He wrote cricket bat.

qa.q: What might Yash have been feeling while he chewed his pencil?
qa.a: Torn between temptation and guilt, though Mahima cannot be sure which feeling was stronger.

qa.q: What other approach could Yash use to decide, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a parent or teacher what they would do, or imagine the money was his own, which makes the owner's need easier to feel.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Yash's decision?
qa.a: Mahima cannot tell what Yash felt, but sees him walk to the office and treats it as a thoughtful choice.

grounding: A boy weighs keeping the found money against the owner's possible needs and his own guilt before deciding.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: keeping it because nobody saw [Pitfall]
passage: The hundred-rupee note lay by the paan stall, curled like a leaf. Bhupen looked left, looked right, and pocketed it. Nobody saw. All morning at school it sat there like a warm stone. At recess Amandeep offered to share chips and Bhupen said no, he was not hungry, though he was. In maths the sums swam. Each time a teacher glanced his way his ears went hot, though nobody asked him anything. That evening he walked back past the paan stall and stared at the empty spot on the pavement. He still had the note in his pocket that night, and no wish to spend it.

qa.q: How much money did Bhupen pick up?
qa.a: He picked up a hundred-rupee note.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling in class?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty, since his ears went hot every time a teacher glanced his way.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do to ease this feeling, and why?
qa.a: He could give the note to the stall owner or a teacher in case the owner returns, which would end the worry that follows him.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have wondered when Bhupen refused the chips?
qa.a: Amandeep may have wondered why Bhupen said he was not hungry, since something seemed to be wrong.

grounding: A boy pockets money because no one saw, and spends the day uneasy, caught by his own guilt rather than by anyone.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
passage: Yesterday in the school yard I found a fifty-rupee note near the water tank. My hand closed on it before my mind decided anything. I wanted a mango bar, but I also thought: somebody is missing this. I did not know what to do, so at home I asked Papa. He put down his tea. "Good that you asked, beti. If someone lost it, they will ask the teacher first. Give it to your class teacher in the morning." So today I gave it to Kamal Sir, who announced it in class. Nobody has come yet, but I felt lighter. - Ruchi

qa.q: How much money did Ruchi find?
qa.a: Ruchi found a fifty-rupee note.

qa.q: What was Ruchi feeling as she held the note?
qa.a: Torn, since Ruchi wanted a mango bar but also felt that somebody was missing the money.

qa.q: What else could Ruchi do if nobody claims the note, and why?
qa.a: Ruchi could ask Kamal Sir or the office how it will be handled, so the person who lost it can still claim it.

qa.q: How does Ruchi's father see her question?
qa.a: He is glad she asked, and he helps her think of the teacher as the person the owner would ask first.

grounding: A girl unsure about keeping fifty rupees asks her father, who suggests giving it to the class teacher.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: reasoning about who could claim it [Thinking]
passage: Ishita and Jasleen were walking home when Jasleen spotted a leather wallet on the pavement and two coins near the drain. "Finders keepers!" said Jasleen. Ishita frowned and thought aloud. "The wallet has cards and a photo. A name is in there, so it belongs to someone, and they're worried right now. The coins... nobody can tell whose, and anyone could have dropped them in a public lane." She picked up the wallet. "The wallet goes to the guard at the society gate, who can call the owner. The coins are nobody's in particular." Jasleen slowly nodded and pocketed nothing.

qa.q: What was inside the wallet?
qa.a: There were cards and a photo inside.

qa.q: What was Ishita thinking about the wallet's owner?
qa.a: Ishita imagined the owner as worried right now, so she felt concern and wanted to trace the person.

qa.q: What other approach could they use if the guard is not at the gate, and why?
qa.a: They could hand the wallet to a shopkeeper, a teacher or the police post, since anyone can help trace an owner from the cards.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see the wallet at first?
qa.a: Jasleen sees a lucky find, as "Finders keepers!" shows, and has not thought about the owner yet.

grounding: A girl reasons that a wallet with cards has a traceable owner while stray coins do not, so the wallet must be handed over.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
passage: Sunday night. I found a wallet at the park and ran to the address on the card inside. The lady, Nandini Aunty, said "Thank you, beta" and shut the door. That was it! No sweets, nothing. I was so angry that I kicked the gate on the way back. At dinner Abbu asked why my face was long. I told them. Ammi said, "Did you return it for a reward, or because it wasn't yours?" I did not know how to answer. Abbu said those two feel different in the belly. I am still cross, but I keep thinking about that. - Yusuf

qa.q: What did Nandini Aunty say when Yusuf returned the wallet?
qa.a: Nandini Aunty said "Thank you, beta" and shut the door.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel after leaving Nandini Aunty's house?
qa.a: Angry and let down, so Yusuf kicked the gate on the way back.

qa.q: What other way could Yusuf think about returning things, and why?
qa.a: Yusuf could see it as simply right because the wallet was not Yusuf's, so a thank-you is enough and the good feeling does not depend on payment.

qa.q: How do Ammi and Abbu see Yusuf's anger?
qa.a: They treat it as a chance to talk gently about why people return things, not as something to scold.

grounding: A child who returns a wallet is upset by a bare thank-you, and the parents discuss honesty for a reward versus honesty for its own sake.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
passage: In the school canteen queue, Sangeeta found a folded hundred-rupee note at the counter's edge. She slid it into her pocket. "I'm keeping it," she whispered to Kashish. "Someone dropped it, so it's mine now." Kashish shrugged, then said, "What if it belongs to someone who has very little? The cleaning didi counts every rupee for her bus fare." Sangeeta's chest felt tight. She thought of the cleaner's tired steps in the corridor. "Fine." At the counter she held out the note. "Canteen Uncle, someone dropped this. Please keep it for whoever asks." He tucked it into a tin and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta find the note?
qa.a: She found it at the counter's edge in the canteen queue.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling after Kashish spoke about the cleaning didi?
qa.a: Uneasy and sympathetic, since her chest felt tight as she pictured the cleaner's tired steps.

qa.q: What else could Sangeeta do so the owner can find the note, and why?
qa.a: She could ask the canteen or a teacher to put up a notice, so whoever lost it knows where to ask.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Sangeeta's plan to keep the note?
qa.a: Kashish shrugs at first, then gently points out that the owner may need it badly, hoping Sangeeta will think again.

grounding: A girl decides to keep found money, then a friend's remark changes her mind and she hands it to the canteen.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: checking for a name or phone number to trace the owner [Action]
passage: Devansh found a black wallet by the school gate after the bell. Instead of guessing whose it was, he carried it to Lavanya Ma'am in the staff room. "Let's look together," she said, opening it on the table with the door wide. Inside were notes, a bus pass and a visiting card with a name and a phone number. Devansh read out the number and Lavanya Ma'am dialled it on the office phone. Within the hour a breathless man in a grey shirt arrived at the gate, counted nothing, and shook Devansh's hand in both of his.

qa.q: What did they find in the wallet that helped trace the owner?
qa.a: They found a visiting card with a name and a phone number.

qa.q: What was Devansh feeling when the man shook his hand?
qa.a: Proud and pleased, since his careful looking through the wallet had brought the owner back.

qa.q: What could they have done if the wallet had held no card, and why?
qa.a: They could have given it to the school office or the police post with a notice, so the owner would know where to claim it.

qa.q: How might the owner have felt when he reached the gate?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since he arrived breathless and shook Devansh's hand in both of his.

grounding: A boy checks a found wallet with his teacher, finds a card with a number, and the owner is reached within the hour.
